title: A Huge (But Secret) Key To Classroom Management Success
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Drawing on his personal coaching practice, Linsin identifies a commonality he says most struggling teachers are unaware of: a lack of alignment between what teachers actually want and what students understand is expected. His three-step fix is to first know precisely what is wanted from students in every moment, since ambiguity gets filled with disruption; second, to explicitly teach and model those expectations in detail rather than assuming students will infer them, noting that specificity is engaging rather than boring; and third, to explain the reasoning behind expectations, since he says buy-in dramatically increases compliance even when the explanation itself isn't airtight. He frames the payoff as flipping who carries the burden of responsibility in a classroom — from an overloaded, stressed teacher narrating everything, to students who feel a real sense of purpose and ownership over their own behavior.
points: A common hidden gap: teachers don't know exactly what they want from students moment to moment, and students fill the gap themselves.
Step one is deciding precisely what is wanted from students for every routine and transition, down to specific details like phone use.
Step two is explicitly teaching and modeling expectations in detail; specificity is engaging to students, not boring.
Step three is explaining why, since buy-in dramatically increases compliance even when the explanation isn't airtight.
The payoff is flipping the burden of responsibility from an overloaded teacher to students who feel real purpose and ownership.
quotes: As part of my personal coaching practice I speak to a lot of teachers.
Most teachers don’t really know what they want and expect from their students from minute to minute, which means the students have to figure it out for themselves.
You must visualize in your mind’s eye how you want your students to pull out their laptops, for example, or clean their instruments or transition to another subject.
Many teachers gloss over nearly everything in the false belief that students will get bored. The opposite is true. Specificity is good teaching.
Studies confirm that when you explain why—even if the why doesn’t make sense—your friends, family, and people around you are more likely to go along with your plans, ideas, and leadership decisions.

Knowing what they are to do from opening bell to dismissal gives students a sense of purpose. It shifts responsibility from you, and having to narrate them and correct them through every this and that, to them, where they can feel empowered.
